title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, runbooks, and team wiki links. It is intended as the canonical reference for SREs and runtime engineers operating Redwood's inference runtime. Read this doc to: understand scheduler policies, reproduce perf regressions, run benchmarks, and follow incident procedures.

Contents (short)
1) Runtime architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling design and configuration
3) Profiling playbook (how-to triage perf problems)
4) Benchmarking suite and reproducible tests
5) Recent release notes (v2.8)
6) Known issues and mitigations
7) Runtime runbooks (incidents)
8) Team wiki and ownership

1) Runtime architecture overview

Short intro: Redwood's serving-runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine combined with a stateless control plane (router/orchestrator) and stateful inference workers. The design prioritizes low tail latency, predictable throughput, and graceful fallback. Components:

- rdm-router (control plane): handles request routing, policy evaluation, and fallbacks. Exposes /v1/generate and internal admin endpoints.
- rdm-scheduler: assigns requests to worker pools based on priority, model compatibility, and batching heuristics.
- rdm-worker: process running CUDA-backed kernels and model runtime (KV cache management, attention kernels, quantized execution). Runs in containers backed by GPU allocation.
- rdm-cache: distributed prefix/KV cache used to serve repeated prefixes and reduce token compute. Redis-backed with local LRU in worker.
- metrics & tracing: Prometheus + OpenTelemetry pipeline, traces stored in Jaeger/Tempo.
\Architecture diagram (text):
- Client -> rdm-router -> rdm-scheduler -> rdm-worker (GPU) -> optional rdm-cache -> response
\SLOs and targets (global):
- P50 token latency: <= 8ms (small models, 512 context)
- P95 request latency: <= 60ms
- P99 request latency: <= 250ms (hosted); Dedicated customers may have stricter targets per contract
- Throughput: measured in tokens/sec per GPU; baseline profiles live in model-catalog/profiles/*
\Operational constraints and invariants:
- Workers must preserve KV cache across short-lived preemptions (checkpoint to local NVMe every 30s)
- Scheduler must never place more than MAX_TOKENS_PER_STEP (config) on a single worker to avoid OOMs
- Fallback chains: if a prioritized pool is saturated for > 2s, router retries with compatible quantized variant
\2) Kernel scheduling design and configuration
\Goals: maximize hardware utilization while protecting tail latency and preventing OOM. The scheduler uses a hybrid policy: priority classes + size-based packing + backpressure signals from workers. Key concepts:

- Priority classes: realtime, production, background
  - realtime: low token count, latency-sensitive routes (PLG free tier demos should NOT use realtime)
  - production: customer traffic with SLAs
  - background: batch jobs, offline reranking
- Preemption: only allowed for background -> production. Production and realtime are non-preemptable except under emergency operator flag.
- Batching window: adaptive, default 6ms for realtime, up to 40ms for background traffic.
- Kernel affinity: some custom fused attention kernels prefer single-stream execution; long sequences use multi-stream pipelining.
\Scheduler config (example YAML):

scheduler:
  priority_classes:
    - name: realtime
      share: 0.2
      max_batch_ms: 6
    - name: production
      share: 0.7
      max_batch_ms: 12
    - name: background
      share: 0.1
      max_batch_ms: 40
  max_tokens_per_worker: 65536
  allow_preemption: true
  preemption_rules:
    background_to_production: true
    background_to_realtime: false

Notes on CUDA / kernel-level decisions:
- Use a single CUDA stream per token-group for small models to reduce synchronization overhead. Use multiple streams and CUDA graphs for long sequences (>= 1024).
- Kernel selection table lives in /deploy/kernels/catalog.yaml; the runtime does a fast-path lookup by (model_arch, seq_len, dtype, gpu_arch).
- For quantized kernels (int4/int8), enable stochastic rounding for safety on smaller GPT-family models; control via KERNEL_QUANT_SAFE=true.
\3) Profiling playbook (how to triage perf problems)
\When you observe a latency regression or throughput drop, follow these steps. Keep stakeholders informed in #runtime-ops Slack.
\Immediate checks (5 minutes)
1. Verify alerts: check Prometheus (query: rate(rdm_worker_request_count[1m])). Check P99 latency panels.
2. Check cluster capacity: `rdmctl pool status --zone=us-west2`
3. Look for recent deployments: `kubectl get deploy -n serving --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 10`
\Collection and profiling (10-60 minutes)
1. Capture a flamegraph for the worker:
   - enable perf capture: `rdmctl debug-capture --worker <id> --duration 60s --type=flamegraph`
   - convert with `perf script` + FlameGraph scripts or use py-spy for Python-bound kernels.
2. GPU-side metrics: `nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1` and `nvprof` (when safe). Also capture NVTX markers (runtime includes NVTX spans when RDM_NVTX=1).
3. Trace end-to-end with distributed tracing (request id): query Jaeger for the trace and expand spans for router/scheduler/worker.
4. Compare kernel selection: `curl http://worker:<port>/admin/kernel-selection?model=gpt-j-6b&seq=1024`
\Common profile patterns and meaning:
- High host CPU time + low GPU utilization: indicates batching loop or scheduler lock contention; inspect scheduler logs for lock waits.
- High GPU SM utilization but low throughput: likely memory bandwidth-bound kernel or inefficient kernel variant. Check kernel catalog selection.
- Spikes in memcpy H2D or D2H: indicates frequent KV cache misses or small-batch host transfers. Consider enabling local caching or larger batching windows.
\Example flamegraph diagnosis snippet:
- If top frames show `batch_assembler::assemble_batches`, then reduce contention by increasing assembler worker threads in config: `batch_assembler_threads: 6`.
\4) Benchmarking suite and reproducible tests
\Purpose: provide repeatable measurements for latency, throughput, memory usage, and cost estimates across model variants and hardware. Benchmarks are stored in /bench/serving-suite. Key scripts and test types:

- micro-bench: measures per-kernel latency and memory for common ops (attention, matmul).
- request-bench: synthetic single-request latency suite (varying seq_len, prompt_len, temperature).
- load-bench: ramp tests for tokens/sec sustained over hours.
- canary-bench: small smoke tests to run during rollouts.
\Run a standard single-model benchmark (example):
\# run request-bench against a dedicated pool
./bench/run_bench.sh --suite=request-bench --model=gpt-j-6b --pool=dedicated-us-west2 --concurrency=8 --duration=300
\Key metrics recorded (Prometheus labels + bench output):
- p50/p95/p99 request latency (ms)
- tokens/sec (sustained)
- GPU memory peak (MiB)
- cost-per-token estimate (USD/token) using cost model in benchmarks/cost-model.yaml
\Result artifacts must include: raw traces, flamegraphs, bench-summary.json, and a short conclusions.md. Store results under /artifacts/bench/YYYY-MM-DD/<run-id>.
\Benchmark guidance:
- Always run with 3 warmup runs before capturing metrics.
- Use realistic prompt shapes from sample-sets/prompt-distributions.yaml.
- For quantization/variant comparisons, keep the same hardware and compare only model binary differences.
\5) Release notes (v2.8)
\Release: serving-runtime v2.8 (released 2027-10-01)
Highlights:
- Kernel catalog v3.2: improved fused attention kernel for A100 and H100, 12-18% throughput improvement on long sequences (>=1024).
- Scheduler: adaptive batching window reduced jitter for production class; new backpressure signals for KV cache thrashing.
- Profiling: NVTX span instrumentation added across token decode path.
- Ops: improved admin endpoint `/admin/kernel-selection` and `/admin/kv-stats`.
\Upgrade notes:
- Rolling upgrade recommended: drain one node at a time. Set `allow_preemption=false` in scheduler during upgrade for critical pools.
- If seeing small regressions on long sequences after upgrade, revert kernel_catalog to v3.1 while we investigate.
\6) Known issues and mitigations
\Issue: OOM when sequence length spikes > 4096 on quantized models
- Symptom: worker restarts with OOM, logs include "cudaMalloc failed"
- Mitigation: enable seq_len_cap in router: `max_seq_len: 4096` or route to a bigger GPU pool. Persist fix by adding a model-profile rule in model-catalog.
\Issue: P99 latency regressions during autoscaling events
- Symptom: bursts of P99 for ~30s following new worker additions
- Mitigation: tune `warmup_grace_period` in autoscaler to 60s; use canary-bench during autoscaling tests.
\Issue: Kernel selection falls back to slower kernel on H100 due to incorrect arch tag
- Symptom: throughput drop ~20% on H100-only pools
- Mitigation: hotfix in /deploy/kernels/catalog.yaml to include h100v2 tag and restart workers. Longer-term: add unit-tests to CI that validate kernel selection per GPU type.
\7) Runtime runbooks (incidents)
\High-level pager flow:
- Pager triggers to #runtime-pager Slack channel and on-call SRE.
- On-call triages using the checklist below.
\Runbook: High tail latency (P99 > 2x SLO)
1. Acknowledge page and create incident doc in /incident/ (template).
2. Check Prometheus dashboards: which pools/models are affected? (panel filters: model, pool, region).
3. Run `rdmctl snapshot --pool <id> --duration 60s` to capture worker metrics.
4. If kernel-bound: enable emergency fallback to compatible CPU-quant variant using `rdmctl route --fallback model:quantized-compat` (limited to 10% traffic).
5. If scheduler contention: temporarily increase `priority_class.share` for production by +10% and watch P99.
6. Notify product/CS if any dedicated customer is impacted.
7. Post-incident: attach flamegraphs, traces, and timeline to the incident doc.
\Runbook: OOM loop on worker
1. Move traffic off worker: `kubectl cordon <node>` and `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets`
2. Inspect worker logs: `/var/log/rdm/worker.log` for cudaMalloc failures.
3. Check model config: max_seq_len and batch size. Reduce `max_concurrent_requests` for that worker class.
4. If persistent, scale pool up with larger GPU types and notify infra to review slot sizing.

\How to contribute
- Fork the doc in Confluence editor, add a short summary at the top about the change, and request review from the runtime-team. For code changes to the kernel catalog, open a PR in infra/kernels and add the `kernel-qa` label.
\Appendix: useful commands and snippets
\# Check pool and worker status
rdmctl pool status --zone=us-west2
\# Capture capture NVTX-enabled perf profile (60s)
rdmctl debug-capture --worker <id> --duration 60s --type=nvtx
\# Run micro-bench for attention kernel
./bench/run_micro.sh --kernel=attention --gpu=A100 --iterations=500
\# Example Prometheus alert (pseudoyaml)
- alert: HighServingP99
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(rdm_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 0.25
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Serving runtime P99 > 250ms across production pools"
\Contact and escalation
If you cannot resolve within 30 minutes, escalate to the on-call senior runtime engineer and SRE manager. For security-sensitive incidents, follow security-and-compliance/incident-response-security page and loop in security@redwood.com.
